solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pilot's direction-finder or mascot adjusted before transfer

indicators.note: before places the rearranged letters ahead of the word for transfer
adjusted says the letters of 'or mascot' are shifted into a new order

parts.note: to pass something is to hand it over or transfer it

explanation.surface: A pilot's instrument, or a mascot tweaked before being handed on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adjusted' turns OR MASCOT into ASTROCOM, placed 'before' the transfer word. The pilot is an aircraft navigator's, fixing direction by the stars.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrocompass is a navigation instrument that finds direction from the stars, used by aircraft navigators.

clue.text: What'll make Scots keener? That is following old king

indicators.note: following says the abbreviation comes after the king's name

parts.note: Saul was the first king of Israel
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, 'that is'

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what would make Scottish people sharper, plus a nod to an ancient king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' comes 'following' the king. 'keener' is not 'more eager': a keener is a professional mourner who wails at a funeral, and in Scotland such a hired mourner was a saulie.
explanation.definitionFit: A saulie is a hired funeral mourner in Scots, and keening is wailing for the dead, so a saulie makes the keening.

clue.text: E.g. basalt for filling course

indicators.note: filling says the word for 'for' is packed inside the word for course

parts.note: a track is a course, as for racing
pro means for, in favour of

explanation.surface: Basalt used as hardcore to fill a track or course bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Traprock is any dark fine-grained igneous rock, basalt being the standard example.

clue.text: Port wine's bottled? Stow to mature thus

indicators.note: bottled is slang for drunk, so the letters of 'Port wine's' are scrambled

parts.note: the letters of Stow are the ones taken out of the scrambled pool

explanation.surface: Port goes into bottles and is put away to age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottled' (drunk) signals a composite anagram: the letters of PORT WINES rearranged are the answer plus the letters of STOW.
explanation.definitionFit: To ripen is to come to full maturity, as fruit or wine laid down does.

clue.text: Poet exchanging recipe for a legume

indicators.note: exchanging recipe for a means the abbreviation of recipe in the poet's name is swapped for the word a

parts.note: William Cowper was an 18th-century English poet
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as on a prescription

explanation.surface: A poet who swaps a recipe for a bean dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchanging recipe for a' swaps R (recipe, from Latin recipe 'take' on prescriptions) for A in COWPER.
explanation.definitionFit: The cowpea, or black-eyed pea, is a bean plant, a member of the legume family.

clue.text: Performing well, Ben maybe loses his first grand (6, two words)

indicators.note: loses his first means the playwright's name drops its opening letter

parts.note: Ben Jonson was the Jacobean playwright, Ben being one example of a Jonson
G is the abbreviation of grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: A performer called Ben is doing well though he loses his first thousand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ben maybe' points to Ben Jonson; 'loses his first' drops the J to give ONSON, and G for grand follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on song is a British idiom for being in top form, performing at your best.

clue.text: The Scots speak indistinctly, low and soft

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do
p (piano) is the musical abbreviation for soft

explanation.surface: Scots mumble in quiet, low voices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low' is the verb for a cow's call, not 'quiet'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moop is a Scots variant of moup, to mumble or nibble, so to speak indistinctly in Scottish usage.

clue.text: Brewed cha coming in I drink up — while playing this?

definitions.text: Brewed cha coming in I drink up — while playing this?

indicators.note: coming in says the brewed tea goes inside the reversed letters
in a down clue, up means read the letters of 'I sip' upwards

parts.note: to sip is to drink

indicators.note: brewed says the letters of cha are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: Tea is brewed and sipped over a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brewed' makes ACH of cha, which goes 'coming in' to PISI, I SIP read 'up'. The whole clue pictures a tea-drinking game, so it doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pachisi is the Indian race game from which ludo derives, where sipping tea while playing would be natural.

clue.text: Military governor has shortened broad cannon?

indicators.note: shortened says one letter is lopped from the gun, cutting SHOT short

parts.note: a shotgun scatters its pellets broadly, so it is a cannon with a broad spread, playfully

explanation.surface: An officer's broad cannon has been cut down.
explanation.walkthrough: The shot of SHOTGUN is 'shortened' by losing its T.
explanation.definitionFit: A shogun was the hereditary military commander who effectively ruled Japan for centuries.

clue.text: A lump of glass for moulding

definitions.text: A lump of glass for moulding

parts.words: A lump of glass for moulding
parts.note: this was the competition word, which solvers were invited to clue, so the printed clue is only its definition

explanation.walkthrough: In Azed competition puzzles one entry is given by definition alone and entrants write the clue, so there is no wordplay here.
explanation.definitionFit: A parison is the gob of molten glass partly shaped before being blown or pressed into its final mould.

clue.text: Curses pipes around start of Hogmanay

indicators.note: around says the pipes enclose the letter that follows

parts.note: oats are straws used as rustic pipes in pastoral poetry

indicators.note: start of takes the first letter of Hogmanay

parts.note: first letter of Hogmanay

explanation.surface: Bagpipes and swearing at a Scottish New Year party.
explanation.walkthrough: OATS goes 'around' H, the 'start of' Hogmanay. An oat is a shepherd's pipe made of an oat straw, a pastoral-poetry sense; Hogmanay is the Scottish New Year's Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: Oaths are swear words, the profane sense of curses.

clue.text: Mats we're given in arrangement for wine glasses, etc

indicators.note: given in arrangement says the letters of 'Mats we're' are reordered

explanation.surface: Table mats laid out alongside the wine glasses.
explanation.definitionFit: Stemware is collective for glasses with stems, chiefly wine glasses and goblets.

clue.text: Their womenfolk will appear leaderless, burying father?

definitions.text: Their womenfolk will appear leaderless, burying father?

indicators.note: burying says the word for father is tucked inside
leaderless drops the opening letter of the women's word

parts.note: squaw is the dated (now offensive) word for a Native American woman
pa is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A tribe's women, leaderless, burying a dead father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaderless' leaves QUAWS, 'burying' father. 'squaw' is a dated, now offensive word for a Native American woman; these are the answer's own women, so the whole clue also defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The Quapaw are a Native American people of the Arkansas region, so their women are fittingly squaws.

clue.text: Bill's other half cut it — silly

definitions.note: here a noun, a silly person, as in 'you big silly'

parts.note: 'bill and coo' is the paired phrase for lovers' cooing, so coo is the other half of bill

indicators.note: cut says the word it is cut short, losing a letter

explanation.surface: A wife cuts her husband Bill's name and calls him silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a man's name, but the idiom is 'bill and coo'; 'cut' trims IT to T.
explanation.definitionFit: A coot is an old-fashioned word for a foolish person, as in 'silly old coot'.

clue.text: Timer with which girl follows say gee-gee (8, two words)

indicators.note: follows puts the girl after the other pieces

parts.note: eg (for example) is signalled by 'say'
GG is the abbreviation for gee-gee, a horse in baby talk
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A girl riding a horse with a stopwatch.
explanation.walkthrough: The girl 'follows' the rest; a gee-gee is British nursery talk for a horse, abbreviated to its two initials.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg glass is a small sandglass that runs for the few minutes needed to boil an egg.

clue.text: Work extremes of hilarity into edited page — part at top or foot of column

definitions.text: part at top or foot of column

indicators.note: into says the work and the outer letters go inside the reworked page
edited says the letters of page are rearranged

parts.note: op (opus) is a musical work

indicators.note: extremes of takes the first and last letters of hilarity

parts.note: first and last letters of hilarity

explanation.surface: A funny column is edited onto a page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edited' page gives APGE, which takes the work and HY, the 'extremes of' hilarity, 'into' it after its second letter. 'column' is architectural, not journalistic.
explanation.definitionFit: An apophyge is the concave curve where an architectural column's shaft meets its base or capital.

clue.text: Ugly expressions from sailors captured by foreign troops

indicators.note: captured by says the sailors sit inside the troops

parts.note: GIs are American soldiers, foreign from a British viewpoint
RN is the Royal Navy, hence sailors

explanation.surface: Sailors held prisoner by an enemy army pull ugly faces.
explanation.walkthrough: RN is 'captured by' GIS; GIs are American soldiers, 'foreign' to a British setter.
explanation.definitionFit: A girn is a snarl or grimace, chiefly in Scots and northern English, so girns are grotesque faces.

clue.text: Bit of of soldier's kit — this set gets miles put out

indicators.note: put out means disturbed or displaced, so the letters of 'miles put' are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of set are the ones that join 'this' answer in the rearranged pool

explanation.surface: A piece of an infantryman's gear, issued as a set, gets miles knocked off.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: 'this' stands for the answer, and with SET it makes the letters of MILES PUT, 'out' signalling the shuffle. Miles is also Latin for a soldier, and the pilum was a Roman one's.
explanation.definitionFit: The pilum was the heavy throwing javelin carried by every Roman legionary.

clue.text: Some duties go on for a long time

parts.note: to last is to go on, to continue
ages means a long time, as in 'it took ages'

explanation.surface: Some jobs drag on interminably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duties' are taxes, not chores.
explanation.definitionFit: Lastage was a toll levied on goods by the last, a load measure, or a port charge, so lastages are tolls of this kind.

clue.text: Wildly eggy about a hop going wrong — sign of mania?

indicators.note: about says the scrambled eggy wraps round the other letters
wildly says the letters of eggy are shaken up
going wrong says the letters of 'a hop' are jumbled

explanation.surface: A manic dance with a wild hop and something eggy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wildly' turns EGGY into GEGY, which goes 'about' OPHA, the letters of A HOP 'going wrong'.
explanation.definitionFit: Geophagy, eating earth or clay, can be a symptom of a disordered mind, hence a possible sign of madness.

clue.text: Guardian of gardens? Matter holding partner up

indicators.note: holding says the matter encloses the reversed partner

parts.note: pus is the yellowish matter of an infected wound

indicators.note: in a down clue, up says the partner word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a pair is a partner, one of a couple

explanation.surface: A gardener's matter holds up a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns PAIR into RIAP, and PUS is 'holding' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Priapus was the Greek fertility god whose statues stood in gardens to guard them against thieves.

clue.text: Its music is hammered out, a lilting strain

indicators.note: lilting, swinging in rhythm, says the letters of strain are swung about

explanation.surface: Music beaten out to a swinging tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lilting' rearranges STRAIN; 'hammered out' sounds like an anagram signal but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A santir is a Persian dulcimer, whose strings are struck with small hammers.

clue.text: Personality one follows is wreathed in allure

indicators.note: follows puts the one after the rest
wreathed in says the word is wrapped inside the allure

parts.note: charm is allure, attractiveness
a means one, as in 'a dozen'

explanation.surface: Someone's personality is wrapped up in their allure.
explanation.definitionFit: Charisma is compelling personal magnetism, the kind of personality that draws others.

clue.text: Put up sort of trough, to employ inside

indicators.note: inside says the word for employ sits within the trough

parts.note: a hod is an open trough on a pole for carrying bricks
to use is to employ

explanation.surface: Putting up a trough so a worker can be employed.
explanation.definitionFit: Housed is to put someone up, providing lodging.

clue.text: Visitor to Italy blowing in from the south, e.g. Paul

definitions.text: Visitor to Italy blowing in from the south
definitions.meaning: first sense: the ..., the Roman name for the south wind
second sense: Paul ..., the American novelist

explanation.surface: A tourist arriving in Italy from the south, maybe a man named Paul.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'visitor' is a wind, not a tourist.
explanation.definitionFit: Auster was Latin for the south wind reaching Italy, and the surname of New York novelist Paul Auster.

clue.text: Like the Carpenter, or his mate, swallowing first of oysters?

indicators.note: swallowing says the mate takes the letter inside

parts.note: the Carpenter's companion in Lewis Carroll's poem is the Walrus, and morse is an old word for walrus

indicators.note: first of takes the opening letter of oysters

parts.note: first letter of oysters

explanation.surface: Carroll's Carpenter and the Walrus gulp down oysters.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass the Walrus and the Carpenter eat the oysters; morse is an old name for the walrus, here 'swallowing' O, the 'first of' oysters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Carpenter is sullen and terse in Carroll's poem, so gloomy fits him.

clue.text: Little old lady is havin' a work break up north

definitions.meaning: first sense: ..., an obsolete diminutive for lady, as in 'by'r ...'

definitions.text: havin' a work break up north
definitions.meaning: second sense: ...', northern dialect for playing or idling off work, from lake, to play

explanation.walkthrough: The dropped g in 'havin'' signals the dialect form laking.
explanation.definitionFit: Lakin was an archaic short form of ladykin, and in Yorkshire to lake is to play or be off work.

clue.text: Player in Milan team, rubbish back

parts.note: AC Milan is the Italian football club

indicators.note: back says the rubbish word is read in reverse

parts.note: rot means nonsense, rubbish

explanation.surface: A footballer for Milan is rubbish on his comeback.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor is a player on stage.

clue.text: It includes Obama's 'Bo', among Americanisms

indicators.note: among says the letters lie within the word Americanisms

parts.note: the letters sit inside the word: ameriCANISms

explanation.surface: Talk of the President's dog among American turns of phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer lies 'among' the letters of Americanisms. Bo was the Obama family's Portuguese water dog in the White House.
explanation.definitionFit: Canis is the genus of dogs and wolves, so it takes in any pet dog.

clue.text: One pill to take as treatment for alcoholism

parts.note: an means one
a tab is a tablet, a pill
to take a thing is to use it

explanation.surface: A doctor's instruction to take one pill for drinking problems.
explanation.definitionFit: Antabuse is the trade name of disulfiram, a drug that makes drinking alcohol unpleasant.

clue.text: Fishing vessel, or smack

explanation.walkthrough: A smack is also a fishing boat, which steers you towards a second vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A buss was a two- or three-masted herring boat, and to buss is to kiss loudly.

clue.text: Portion of ripest apples and stuff that's gone

indicators.note: portion of says the letters are a part taken from 'ripest apples'

parts.note: the letters run across the words: ripeST APples

explanation.surface: Some overripe apples and leftovers past their best.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a 'Portion of' ripest apples; 'that's gone' marks the sense as obsolete.
explanation.definitionFit: Stap is an obsolete or dialect word meaning to cram or fill tight, a vanished verb for stuffing.

clue.text: Tossing off strong drinks

indicators.note: off, as in gone wrong, says the letters of Tossing are disordered

explanation.surface: Knocking back strong drinks in one go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tossing off' looks like gulping a drink down, but 'off' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingo is an old word for strong beer or ale.

clue.text: Positions befit me (as editor might put it)

parts.note: to sit is an old sense meaning to suit or befit
an editor writes with the editorial 'we', so me becomes us

explanation.surface: These arrangements suit me, as an editor might say.
explanation.walkthrough: The editorial 'we' turns 'me' into US.
explanation.definitionFit: Situs is the Latin-derived word for situation or location, used in law and anatomy.

clue.text: Extremely weird lake in east of France

indicators.note: in places the lake inside the French word

parts.note: est is French for east
Erie is one of the North American Great Lakes

explanation.surface: A spooky lake in eastern France.
explanation.walkthrough: ERIE goes 'in' EST; 'east of France' is the French word for east, not a region of France.
explanation.definitionFit: Eeriest is the superlative of eerie, strange and unsettling.

clue.text: Perry maybe balancing on sideboard

indicators.note: on places the first piece above the furniture, as in a down light

parts.note: cross can mean reciprocal or counterbalancing, as cross entries in accounts offset each other
a dresser is a sideboard with shelves

explanation.surface: A pot by Perry sits poised on a sideboard.
explanation.walkthrough: CROSS goes 'on' DRESSER. Grayson Perry, the British potter, often appears as his female alter ego Claire.
explanation.definitionFit: Artist Grayson Perry is a famous transvestite, someone who wears clothes of the other sex.
